paragraphs: Measuring a model's performance requires knowing when its predictions are wrong, which becomes expensive when obtaining correct labels costs time or money. This paper studies how to estimate performance while requesting relatively few labels. The evaluation process actively chooses what to label, making label selection part of the estimation problem.

Active Surrogate Estimators use a learned stand-in to estimate prediction errors for examples whose labels remain unknown. Rather than forming a Monte Carlo estimator, they interpolate these errors through the surrogate. The method actively improves this surrogate as labels become available. Its acquisition strategy, XWED, selects information with the final performance estimate in mind, aligning what the surrogate learns with the evaluation task.

On challenging evaluations of deep neural networks, the authors report greater label efficiency than the existing state of the art. The finding supports learning where errors occur as a useful route to economical evaluation. Its significance is about spending a limited labeling budget more effectively when measuring an existing model's performance.
neurips-2022-active-surrogate-estimators.tldr: Active Surrogate Estimators learn to estimate errors on unlabeled examples, improving label efficiency in the reported model evaluations.

paragraphs: Click-through rate prediction estimates whether a user will click an item in a web application. Conventional deep models use the same learned network parameters for every example. The authors argue that this fixed treatment limits how well a model can represent examples arising from different underlying distributions.

The Adaptive Parameter Generation network, or APG, generates model parameters dynamically according to the instance being processed. This makes instance-specific adaptation part of prediction itself. APG is presented as a module that can be incorporated into different deep click-through rate models, and the reported experiments show significant performance improvements across a variety of those models.

The paper also reports efficiency and deployment results. Compared with a regular deep click-through rate model, APG can reduce time cost by 38.7% and memory use by 96.6%. In an industrial sponsored search deployment, it achieved a 3% click-through rate gain and a 1% RPM gain. These results show that the tested form of adaptive parameter generation improved prediction while also offering substantial resource savings in the reported comparison.
neurips-2022-apg-adaptive-parameter-gene.tldr: APG generates instance-specific parameters for click prediction, with reported gains in predictive performance, efficiency, and industrial deployment.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether showing intermediate reasoning in a prompt helps language models solve problems that require several steps. The proposed method supplies a few worked examples containing a sequence of reasoning steps. These demonstrations give the model examples of how to develop an answer through intermediate conclusions.

The authors find that this prompting approach can elicit reasoning abilities in sufficiently large language models. Experiments with three large models show improvements across arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. The qualification about size matters: the stated finding concerns abilities emerging in sufficiently large models, rather than an unconditional benefit for every language model.

A highlighted result uses eight worked examples to prompt a model with 540 billion parameters. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on GSM8K math word problems, exceeding even a fine-tuned GPT-3 system equipped with a verifier. The broader contribution is evidence that the structure of demonstrations can substantially affect measured reasoning performance. In the reported settings, including intermediate steps makes prompting a powerful way to draw out capabilities.
neurips-2022-chain-of-thought-prompting-.tldr: Worked reasoning examples in prompts substantially improve sufficiently large language models' performance on several reasoning tasks.

paragraphs: Language models can produce text that is toxic, biased, false, or otherwise harmful. Anticipating these harms does not automatically produce a rigorous way to measure them. This paper addresses that translation problem: how concerns about potential harm can inform the design of benchmarks that evaluate language models.

The authors outline six characteristics of harmful text that deserve explicit attention during benchmark design. They then use those characteristics to examine existing benchmarks, identifying patterns in what evaluations cover and gaps in their coverage. This gives the proposed framework a practical role in assessing how current measurement choices relate to the harms researchers want to study.

The paper also applies the framework to the Perspective API, a toxicity classifier commonly used within harm benchmarks. That case study connects the discussion to a concrete evaluation component. The contribution is a set of considerations for making benchmark design more deliberate and examining existing evaluations more systematically. The authors position it as one part of the connection between anticipating harms and evaluating them effectively.
neurips-2022-characteristics-of-harmful-.tldr: The paper proposes six characteristics of harmful text to guide benchmark design and examine gaps in existing language-model evaluations.

paragraphs: Temporal point processes model discrete events occurring in continuous time. This paper asks how such models can answer a different kind of question: given the events that actually occurred, what might have happened under an alternative event intensity? This is relevant when event models help inform targeted interventions.

The authors construct a causal model of thinning, an event-selection process, using the Gumbel-Max structural causal model. Their construction satisfies counterfactual monotonicity, a condition sufficient to identify counterfactual dynamics within thinning. They combine that causal model with the superposition theorem to build a sampling algorithm. Starting from an observed event sequence and its intensity function, the algorithm simulates counterfactual sequences under a specified alternative intensity.

Experiments use synthetic data and real epidemiological data to explore the resulting counterfactual realizations. The results suggest that these simulations may provide useful insights for targeted interventions. The contribution links observed event histories to alternative scenarios through an explicit causal construction, with the identification claim grounded in the stated sufficient condition.
neurips-2022-counterfactual-temporal-poi.tldr: A causal thinning model enables sampling counterfactual event sequences under alternative intensity functions.

paragraphs: Learning agents for difficult sequential decisions often depends on both interactive environments and large collections of demonstrations. Access to suitable data and the cost of processing it can constrain research. This paper introduces the NetHack Learning Dataset, using a game that is challenging for current methods while being fast to run.

The dataset brings together human and automated play. Its human portion contains 10 billion state transitions from 1.5 million trajectories collected on the public NAO server between 2009 and 2020. Its bot portion contains 3 billion state-action-score transitions from 100,000 trajectories produced by the symbolic bot that won the NetHack Challenge 2021. Accompanying code supports recording, loading, and streaming trajectories in highly compressed form.

The authors evaluate a broad range of existing demonstration-learning algorithms on this resource. Their results indicate that substantial research advances are still needed to make full use of large datasets for difficult sequential decisions. The contribution therefore combines accessible data and processing tools with evidence of a continuing gap between having demonstrations at scale and learning effectively from them.
neurips-2022-dungeons-and-data-a-large-s.tldr: The NetHack Learning Dataset supplies billions of human and bot transitions, exposing challenges in learning effectively from large demonstration datasets.

paragraphs: Predicting where a person will move is difficult because human choices are variable. The paper starts from a qualified hypothesis: in constrained scenes, layouts, obstacles, and interactions create recurring movement patterns, so another person may already have traveled a similar future route. It calls the regularities derived from past movement and environmental interactions scene history.

The proposed Scene History Excavating Network, SHENet, uses two forms of that history. A group trajectory bank extracts representative routes as candidates for future movement. A cross-modal interaction module then relates the individual's previous trajectory to their surroundings to refine the prediction. Together, these components connect recurring paths in a scene with information specific to the person being forecast.

The authors also propose including smoothness in evaluation metrics to mitigate uncertainty associated with randomness and subjective choices. Evaluations on ETH, UCY, and the new PAV benchmark show superior performance relative to the compared state-of-the-art methods. These results support using historical scene regularities as useful predictive evidence under the paper's movement-pattern hypothesis.
neurips-2022-forecasting-human-trajector.tldr: SHENet forecasts movement using representative historical paths and person-surroundings interactions, with superior results on the reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how neural signed distance functions can represent three-dimensional objects from unseen, unlabeled point clouds. The central challenge is transferring learned shape knowledge to new categories. Existing methods can offer detailed reconstructions or fast inference within a small collection of classes, yet struggle to generalize to unfamiliar shapes.

GenSDF addresses this through two stages of semi-supervised meta-learning. The first stage uses training episodes that simulate learning from unlabeled data, developing initial shape priors. The second stage introduces unlabeled examples from disjoint classes, broadening those priors. This arrangement transfers knowledge from labeled examples while exposing the model to additional categories without requiring labels for those examples.

The authors evaluate the approach on synthetic data and real collected point clouds. They report better performance than existing neural signed distance function methods and robust zero-shot inference across more than 100 unseen classes. The stated findings support the value of diversifying learned shape priors: the model can use its training experience to reconstruct categories beyond those for which labeled examples were provided.
neurips-2022-gensdf-two-stage-learning-o.tldr: GenSDF combines two stages of semi-supervised meta-learning to reconstruct unfamiliar shapes, reporting robust zero-shot inference on over 100 unseen classes.

paragraphs: Smartphones and wearables capture behavioral signals that can support models of people's well-being over time. However, evaluating a model within one population over a short period leaves an important question unresolved: whether it also works for different people or different years. GLOBEM supplies data intended to make those comparisons possible.

The collection contains more than 700 user-years of passive mobile and wearable sensing data from 497 distinct users, together with a range of well-being measures. Its multi-year structure supports multiple evaluations across datasets. This gives researchers an open testbed for comparing algorithms under changes in users and time, extending evaluation beyond a single population observed briefly.

As an initial benchmark, the authors evaluate 18 algorithms on depression detection. Both previous depression detection approaches and domain generalization techniques show promise, but the results indicate that further research is needed for adequate generalization across datasets. The resource's significance lies in making that transfer problem measurable and providing initial evidence that existing approaches have not yet resolved it.
neurips-2022-globem-dataset-multi-year-d.tldr: GLOBEM provides multi-year sensing data to test behavioral models across users and years, revealing remaining generalization challenges in depression detection.

paragraphs: Whether an optimization algorithm is optimal depends on the class of functions it must handle. This paper studies functions satisfying two particular conditions: a lower restricted secant inequality and an upper error bound. The authors are motivated by earlier concerns that the usual assumptions of strong convexity and smoothness can produce pathological condition numbers.

The selected class avoids the cited pathology and includes some nonconvex functions. A key technical finding concerns interpolation: determining whether sampled points and their gradients could belong to a function in this class. The necessary and sufficient requirements separate into simple conditions on each sampled gradient. That structure lets the authors solve the associated performance estimation problem analytically.

The resulting lower bound on convergence establishes that gradient descent is exactly optimal among first-order algorithms on this function class. This is a worst-case statement tied to the specified assumptions. Its significance is that a basic optimization method reaches the best possible convergence rate for this class, with the proof made possible by its unusually tractable geometric conditions.
neurips-2022-gradient-descent-is-optimal.tldr: Gradient descent is exactly optimal among first-order algorithms for functions satisfying the paper's two specified geometric conditions.

paragraphs: Commercial machine-learning APIs make prediction services easy to incorporate into applications, but providers can differ in performance and change their underlying models over time. HAPI records those services' outputs so researchers can compare providers and examine how an individual service evolves.

The dataset contains 1,761,417 API application instances spanning 2020 to 2022, including services from Amazon, Google, IBM, Microsoft, and others. Tasks include image tagging, speech recognition, and text mining. Each instance pairs the query input with the service's prediction or annotation and confidence scores. This makes the collection a resource for studying machine learning as a service across tasks and time.

The authors demonstrate that several APIs lost accuracy on particular benchmark datasets. They also find that stable aggregate performance can conceal changes in which data subtypes produce errors. Such shifts can affect larger analytics pipelines that depend on an API. Additional analyses examine performance disparities across demographic groups over time. Together, these uses show why a single overall accuracy measurement may provide an incomplete picture of an evolving service.
neurips-2022-hapi-a-large-scale-longitud.tldr: HAPI tracks commercial ML API predictions over time, revealing accuracy changes and shifting error patterns that aggregate performance can conceal.

paragraphs: This paper examines a route for covertly transmitting private machine-learning datasets through a neural network intended for publication. The proposed scheme, Cans, uses the network as a carrier while preserving nearly all of its ordinary task utility. The research demonstrates how a published model can carry information beyond its intended predictive function.

Cans makes use of the carrier's learning capacity through a parameter-sharing mechanism. Existing schemes described in the abstract instead treat model parameters as strings of bits. The proposed approach can place multiple heterogeneous datasets within one carrier model. It also includes redundancy designed to preserve the hidden information through common model post-processing performed before publication.

In the reported evaluations, Cans transmits more than 10,000 real-world samples using a carrier with 220 times fewer parameters than the total size of the transmitted data. The authors report distortion below 10^-5 and carrier utility loss below 1%. These findings demonstrate substantial covert data capacity in the evaluated models, together with resilience to the common post-processing techniques considered in the work.
neurips-2022-house-of-cans-covert-transm.tldr: Cans exploits a neural network's learning capacity to covertly carry multiple private datasets with little reported loss of model utility.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when an agent must commit in advance to a schedule of policy updates. That restriction matters when changing a policy adaptively is costly. The setting uses finite-horizon Markov decision processes, and the goal is to learn effectively while keeping the number of update batches small.

For S states, A actions, horizon H, and K episodes, the authors give a computationally efficient algorithm with near-optimal regret scaling as the square root of SAH³K, apart from logarithmic and confidence factors. It needs only O(H + log₂ log₂ K) batches. Its technical ingredients are an exploration design for states that remain insufficiently learned and an efficient way to explore selected directions using an approximate transition model.

The paper also establishes a lower bound on the batches required to obtain square-root-in-K regret with polynomial dependence on the other problem sizes. That bound matches the algorithm's batch requirement up to logarithmic terms. Together, the results characterize how infrequently policies can be updated while retaining the targeted learning performance.
neurips-2022-near-optimal-regret-bounds-.tldr: An efficient reinforcement-learning algorithm achieves near-optimal regret with a small, predetermined number of policy-update batches.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns policies from historical data without collecting additional interactions during training. The authors argue that common benchmarks can make this task unlike deployment: their data may be overly exploratory, their reference policies weak, and their procedures missing policy validation. Real systems may supply only narrowly distributed data collected conservatively for safety.

NeoRL is designed around those concerns. Its datasets use more conservative collection strategies, and its evaluation process includes offline training and offline validation before an online test. The benchmark also emphasizes whether a learned policy improves on the behavior policy already operating the system. This connects algorithm evaluation to the practical question of whether replacing an existing policy is worthwhile.

Experiments find that some recent offline reinforcement-learning algorithms are less competitive than behavior cloning and the deterministic behavior policy. The authors also find that current offline policy evaluation methods struggle to select the best policy. These results suggest that success on earlier benchmarks may overstate effectiveness in realistic settings, and they highlight policy selection as a substantive part of the deployment problem.
neurips-2022-neorl-a-near-real-world-ben.tldr: NeoRL tests offline reinforcement learning with conservative data and explicit validation, exposing weaknesses in some algorithms and policy-selection methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies online control with quadratic losses in a nonstochastic setting. It evaluates the learner against a sequence of disturbance-action policies selected in hindsight to accommodate changing conditions. This dynamic comparison allows the reference policy to change over time, and total variation measures how much that sequence changes.

The authors provide an efficient algorithm whose dynamic policy regret depends on both the time horizon and that total variation. The stated rate has a one-third-power dependence on the horizon and a two-thirds-power variation term, with logarithmic factors suppressed. It improves the previously known square-root rate for general convex losses and is information-theoretically optimal for the LQR setting considered.

The approach uses a reduction from LQR control to online linear regression with delayed feedback. It also introduces a proper learning algorithm achieving optimal dynamic regret with one-third-power horizon dependence on a family of minibatched quadratic losses. The result shows how the structure of quadratic control losses supports sharper guarantees against changing comparison policies than the cited general convex-loss bound.
neurips-2022-optimal-dynamic-regret-in-l.tldr: An efficient online LQR algorithm achieves an optimal dynamic regret rate against changing disturbance-action policies.

paragraphs: Deepfake detectors can work well when test images resemble their training data yet struggle with unfamiliar kinds of forgery. This paper addresses that generalization problem by allowing the detector to adapt to an individual test image before making its prediction. The adaptation task is constructed specifically for that image.

The method synthesizes pseudo-training samples from each test image and uses them to define a temporary training objective. The detector is updated on that objective before evaluating the image. Meta-learning prepares the model for this procedure so that a fast, single gradient-descent step can be sufficient for good detection performance. The authors call this one-shot test-time training, or OST.

Across several benchmark datasets, the approach performs favorably against existing methods when handling unseen data and different post-processing operations. These findings support preparing detectors to make small, sample-specific adjustments at evaluation time. The single-step design is central to the proposal: the training procedure aims to make a brief adaptation useful for the particular image the model is about to assess.
neurips-2022-ost-improving-generalizatio.tldr: OST adapts a deepfake detector to each test image with a single learned update, improving generalization in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Finding an optimal correlated equilibrium in a sequential game can be computationally hard. This paper examines communication and certification equilibria, where a mediator can send messages, receive messages, and remember them. It asks how these communication capabilities affect the difficulty of selecting an equilibrium that optimizes an objective such as welfare.

The authors construct a polynomial-size game that explicitly includes the mediator's actions and decisions. This yields polynomial-time algorithms for optimal communication equilibria and, under an additional assumption, certification equilibria. By varying the mediator's information and the players' permissions to lie or deviate, the framework represents a broader family of equilibrium notions.

Within this family, some familiar notions correspond to a mediator with imperfect recall. The analysis identifies that memory restriction as the driver of computational hardness among the notions considered. The construction also recovers earlier algorithms as special cases. A full-certification version, where players may remain silent but cannot lie about their information, is especially scalable, and experiments on standard benchmark games support the theoretical claims.
neurips-2022-polynomial-time-optimal-equ.tldr: Explicitly modeling a mediator yields polynomial-time optimal communication equilibria and, under an additional assumption, certification equilibria.

paragraphs: A crystal can be modeled as a repeating set of atomic centers, with rigidly moved versions representing the same structure. Ambiguous representations make reliable comparison difficult and allow duplicate or nearly duplicate entries to accumulate in materials databases. This paper develops descriptors intended to make those comparisons both dependable and fast.

The proposed Pointwise Distance Distribution, or PDD, represents a point set as a numerical matrix. It is an invariant, so equivalent structures do not become false negatives merely through their representation. PDD has near-linear computational complexity and an exactly computable comparison metric. The strongest theoretical result is generic completeness for finite and periodic point sets in any dimension: the absence of false positives is qualified as generic, rather than universal.

The authors demonstrate practical scale through more than 200 billion pairwise comparisons of periodic structures in the Cambridge Structural Database, completed over two days on a modest desktop. This combines a theoretical account of discrimination with evidence that the representation can support very large collections of structural comparisons.
neurips-2022-resolving-the-data-ambiguit.tldr: Pointwise Distance Distributions support fast crystal comparisons with invariant descriptors and a generic completeness guarantee.

paragraphs: Images and object shapes can be represented as points on curved mathematical spaces called manifolds. Producing a private estimate from such data requires attention to that geometry because the usefulness of the result depends on compatibility with the space. This paper focuses on privately estimating the Fréchet mean, which minimizes the sum of squared distances to sample points.

The authors develop a K-norm gradient mechanism on Riemannian manifolds. It favors candidate outputs whose objective gradients are close to zero, connecting the private estimate to the optimization condition defining the mean. For positively curved manifolds, using gradients of squared distances provides better control of sensitivity than the Laplace mechanism considered in the paper.

Numerical results on shapes of corpus callosa illustrate that positive-curvature comparison. Further examples examine the mechanism on a sphere and on the manifold of symmetric positive definite matrices. The contribution is a geometry-aware route to private averaging, with the stated sensitivity advantage tied specifically to the positively curved setting and utility illustrated across several structured spaces.
neurips-2022-shape-and-structure-preserv.tldr: A gradient-based privacy mechanism estimates means on manifolds, offering better sensitivity control in the positively curved setting studied.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks use discrete internal representations and have shown insensitivity to small random disturbances. This paper investigates their robustness against deliberately constructed adversarial perturbations. It considers how different training methods and the temporal dimension of spiking networks affect their vulnerability.

The authors construct attacks using different differentiable approximations and derive a Lipschitz constant tailored to spike representations to analyze the robustness retained by these networks. They then propose regularized adversarial training with low computational overhead. The training scheme constrains how much differences between perturbed spike representations can amplify and promotes generalization across multiple adversarial neighborhoods.

On image-recognition benchmarks, the method defends against strong attacks built using differentiable approximations. The authors specifically report that black-box Projected Gradient Descent attacks become nearly ineffective in their experiments. These findings provide empirical support for the proposed training scheme alongside a theoretical analysis of spike-level sensitivity. The reported protection is associated with the evaluated attacks and training method, while the paper's motivation is to make spiking networks more suitable for applications where robustness matters.
neurips-2022-snn-rat-robustness-enhanced.tldr: SNN-RAT combines spike-specific robustness analysis with regularized adversarial training to improve resistance to the evaluated attacks.

paragraphs: Stochastic monotone inclusion problems arise in applications including robust regression and adversarial learning. Their solvers work with stochastic operator evaluations, and the paper measures computational effort by how many such evaluations are needed to reach a specified accuracy. The goal is to reduce that evaluation cost.

The authors introduce variants of stochastic Halpern iteration with recursive variance reduction. Under cocoercivity, and more generally in the Lipschitz-monotone setting, the method reaches an operator norm of epsilon using O(1/epsilon³) evaluations. Existing solvers cited for these same problem classes require O(1/epsilon⁴). The improved exponent means the stated evaluation bound grows more slowly as the desired tolerance becomes smaller.

A further result combines one variant with scheduled restarts. Under additional sharpness or strong monotonicity assumptions, the evaluation requirement becomes O(log(1/epsilon)/epsilon²). These stronger assumptions are part of that faster guarantee. The paper thus gives improved complexity results at two levels of problem structure, showing how variance reduction and, when justified, restarts can reduce the stochastic evaluations needed for accuracy.
neurips-2022-stochastic-halpern-iteratio.tldr: Variance-reduced stochastic Halpern methods improve evaluation complexity, with faster guarantees under additional sharpness or strong monotonicity assumptions.

paragraphs: Non-contrastive self-supervised methods can learn useful representations even when their objectives admit trivial collapsed solutions. This paper investigates how a prediction head helps make that possible. Empirically, the authors find that an identity-initialized head with only its off-diagonal entries trainable still supports competitive representations despite those trivial optima remaining available.

The theoretical analysis identifies substitution and acceleration effects. Substitution allows learning a strong feature in some neurons to stand in for learning it in other neurons through changes to the prediction head. Acceleration allows the substituted features to help weaker features learn faster, reducing the tendency for those weaker features to be ignored.

Together, these effects enable more diverse learned features. The authors suggest that concentrating on the strongest features is likely a cause of dimensional collapse, so the proposed mechanisms offer an explanation for avoiding that behavior. They also provide what they describe as the first end-to-end optimization guarantee for non-contrastive learning with nonlinear networks, a trainable prediction head, and normalization. The contribution connects a particular empirical head configuration to an account of how learning dynamics promote feature diversity.
neurips-2022-the-mechanism-of-prediction.tldr: The paper identifies substitution and acceleration effects through which a trainable prediction head promotes diverse self-supervised features.

paragraphs: Proximal Policy Optimization, or PPO, is widely used in reinforcement learning but has been less common in multi-agent systems. One reason is the belief that its on-policy learning is substantially less sample efficient than off-policy alternatives. This paper tests that belief in settings where multiple agents cooperate.

The study evaluates PPO-based methods in particle-world environments, the StarCraft multi-agent challenge, Hanabi, and Google Research Football. The methods use minimal hyperparameter tuning and no domain-specific algorithmic changes or architectures. Across these testbeds, PPO often matches or exceeds competitive off-policy methods in both final returns and sample efficiency.

The authors also use ablation studies to examine which implementation choices and hyperparameters are critical to empirical performance. They turn these findings into practical recommendations. The result supports simple PPO-based methods as strong baselines when those practices are followed. Its significance is that a broadly applicable algorithm can be highly competitive across several cooperative settings, and that careful implementation materially affects the comparison with more commonly used alternatives.
neurips-2022-the-surprising-effectivenes.tldr: With suitable implementation practices, PPO is often competitive or superior to off-policy methods across four cooperative multi-agent testbeds.

paragraphs: Full self-attention has quadratic cost, while existing sparse alternatives can sacrifice adaptability or retain quadratic training work. SBM-Transformer addresses both concerns by letting each attention head choose an input-dependent pattern of connections. The method equips each head with a mixed-membership stochastic block model.

For each input, a head samples a bipartite graph whose edges determine the attention mask. A straight-through estimator allows predictive-loss gradients to pass through the discrete sampling operation and update edge probabilities. Both forward and backward costs scale linearly with the number of edges, and the head can vary that number according to the input. This makes the chosen connectivity relevant to both information flow and computational cost.

The authors prove universal approximation of arbitrary sequence-to-sequence functions in expectation over the graph distribution. That expectation qualification is part of the theoretical result. Experiments on LRA and GLUE show better performance than the compared efficient attention variants and the original full-attention Transformer. The paper combines a learned sparse computation structure with theoretical expressiveness and reported benchmark gains.
neurips-2022-transformers-meet-stochasti.tldr: SBM-Transformer learns input-dependent attention graphs whose training and inference costs scale with their selected edges.

paragraphs: Online videos contain many demonstrations of sequential behavior but usually lack the action labels needed for imitation learning. Video PreTraining addresses this gap with a semi-supervised pipeline. A small labeled dataset trains an inverse dynamics model, which then supplies action labels for a much larger collection of online Minecraft videos.

The automatically labeled videos train a general behavioral prior using the native mouse-and-keyboard interface at 20 Hz. The resulting agent exhibits meaningful capabilities without task-specific fine-tuning. It can also be adapted through imitation learning or reinforcement learning to difficult exploration tasks that the authors report cannot be learned from scratch through reinforcement learning in their setting.

The models achieve human-level performance on many tasks, and the authors report the first computer agents able to craft diamond tools. They contextualize this achievement as a task that can require proficient humans more than 20 minutes, or 24,000 environment actions. The contribution demonstrates how limited action-labeled data can unlock much larger video collections for learning behavior and provide a useful starting point for demanding sequential tasks.
neurips-2022-video-pretraining-vpt-learn.tldr: VPT uses a small action-labeled dataset to label online Minecraft videos and train agents with useful transferable behavior.
